meta.title: Cost–volume–profit analysis
meta.summary: Contribution margin, the breakeven point, target income before and after tax, using CVP for decisions and sensitivity analysis, cost structure and operating leverage, and multiple products with a sales mix.

videos.title: Contribution margin
videos.take: Contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs; it covers fixed costs, then produces profit

scenes.say: How many e-bikes must Tallgrass sell to make a profit? Cost–volume–profit analysis starts with one idea: contribution margin.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass Trail e-bike
scenes.say: The Trail e-bike sells for $2,400. Variable costs, frame, motor, battery, assembly labor and dealer commission, are $1,500. Each bike contributes $900 toward fixed costs and profit. That's a contribution margin ratio of thirty-seven and a half percent.

scenes.heading: Contribution income statement, 900 bikes
scenes.say: At nine hundred bikes, revenue is $2,160,000, variable costs $1,350,000, and contribution margin $810,000. After $540,000 of fixed costs, operating income is $270,000.

scenes.heading: CVP assumptions
items: Costs split cleanly into fixed and variable
Behavior is linear within the relevant range
Price, unit costs and sales mix are known
scenes.say: CVP assumes costs split cleanly into fixed and variable parts, behave linearly within the relevant range, that selling price, unit costs and the mix of products are known, and that production equals sales.
The power of contribution margin: every extra bike sold adds $900 to operating income, as long as fixed costs don't change.

scenes.q: A cargo bike sells for $3,600 with variable costs of $2,100. What is its contribution margin ratio?
scenes.say: Quick check. A cargo bike sells for thirty-six hundred with variable costs of twenty-one hundred. What's the contribution margin ratio? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. Fifteen hundred divided by thirty-six hundred is about forty-one point seven percent.

videos.title: The breakeven point
videos.take: Breakeven units = fixed costs ÷ unit contribution margin; breakeven revenue = fixed costs ÷ CM ratio

scenes.say: Breakeven is where operating income is exactly zero. Below it Tallgrass loses money; above it, it makes money.
Breakeven in units is fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit. Breakeven in revenue is fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass breakeven
scenes.say: Fixed costs of $540,000 divided by $900 per bike: six hundred bikes to break even. In revenue, $540,000 divided by thirty-seven and a half percent: $1,440,000. Six hundred bikes at $2,400 confirms it.

The equation method gives the same answer: set price times quantity, minus variable cost times quantity, minus fixed costs, equal to zero. Twenty-four hundred Q minus fifteen hundred Q minus five hundred forty thousand equals zero, so Q is six hundred.

scenes.big: A planning tool, not a goal
scenes.say: Breakeven isn't a target. It tells managers how risky a plan is: how far sales can fall before losses start.

scenes.q: If fixed costs rise to $630,000, what is breakeven?
scenes.say: Quick check. If fixed costs rise to six hundred thirty thousand, what's breakeven? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. 630,000 divided by 900 is seven hundred bikes.

videos.title: Target income and taxes
videos.take: Units for a target = (fixed costs + target operating income) ÷ unit CM; gross up net income for taxes

scenes.say: Breaking even isn't the goal. How many bikes for a target profit, before or after tax?

scenes.heading: Target operating income $180,000
scenes.say: To earn $180,000 of operating income, Tallgrass must cover fixed costs plus the target: $720,000. Divided by $900 a bike, that's eight hundred bikes.
If the target is net income after taxes, first convert it to operating income: divide by one minus the tax rate.

scenes.heading: Target net income $150,000, tax 25%
scenes.say: Ana's board wants $150,000 of net income, with a twenty-five percent tax rate. That needs $200,000 of operating income. Fixed costs plus $200,000, divided by $900, is eight hundred twenty-two point two, so Tallgrass must sell eight hundred twenty-three bikes.
Notice that taxes don't change the breakeven point. With zero operating income there's no tax to pay.

scenes.q: Target operating income $90,000. Bikes needed at $900 CM and $540,000 fixed costs?
scenes.say: Quick check. Target operating income ninety thousand. How many bikes? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. 630,000 divided by 900 is seven hundred.

videos.title: Decisions and sensitivity
videos.take: Use CVP to test decisions; margin of safety shows how far sales can fall before losses

scenes.say: CVP really earns its keep when managers ask 'what if'. Here's how Ana tests decisions and risk.

scenes.heading: Spend $30,000 more on advertising?
scenes.say: Marketing wants $30,000 more for advertising and expects forty more sales. Forty bikes times $900 is $36,000 of extra contribution. Less the $30,000, operating income rises by $6,000. Worth it, if the forty sales are realistic.

scenes.heading: Cut price to $2,250 to sell 1,000?
scenes.say: Sales also suggests cutting the price to $2,250 to sell a thousand bikes. Contribution margin falls to $750 a bike, and total contribution to $750,000, $60,000 less than now. Reject it.
The margin of safety is how far sales can fall below budget before Tallgrass loses money: budgeted revenue minus breakeven revenue.

scenes.heading: Margin of safety at 900 bikes
scenes.say: With nine hundred bikes budgeted, the margin of safety is $720,000, or a third of budgeted sales.

scenes.q: Raising the price to $2,500 cuts volume from 900 to 820 bikes. Operating income change?
scenes.say: Quick check. Raising the price to twenty-five hundred cuts volume from nine hundred to eight hundred twenty. What's the change in operating income? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. Contribution becomes 820 times $1,000, or $820,000, against $810,000 now: up $10,000.

videos.title: Cost structure and operating leverage
videos.take: More fixed costs mean higher operating leverage: bigger swings in income when sales change

scenes.say: Two companies with the same profit can carry very different risk. The difference is cost structure.
The degree of operating leverage is contribution margin divided by operating income. It tells you how much operating income changes for each percent change in sales.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass at 900 bikes
scenes.say: At nine hundred bikes, Tallgrass's contribution margin is $810,000 and operating income $270,000: a degree of operating leverage of three. A ten percent rise in sales raises operating income by thirty percent.

scenes.heading: Automate assembly?
scenes.say: Ana is considering a robotic assembly line. Variable cost would fall to $1,300 a bike, but fixed costs would rise to $720,000. At nine hundred bikes, income is the same, $270,000. But breakeven rises to about six hundred fifty-five bikes.
With more fixed costs, the robotic line earns more when sales beat nine hundred and loses more when they fall short. The choice depends on how confident Ana is about volume.

scenes.q: With a DOL of 4, sales fall 5%. What happens to operating income?
scenes.say: Quick check. With a degree of operating leverage of four, sales fall five percent. What happens to operating income? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Four times five percent: a twenty percent fall.

videos.title: Multiple products and sales mix
videos.take: With several products, compute breakeven for a bundle in the expected sales mix

scenes.say: Tallgrass sells two bikes, not one. With several products, breakeven depends on the sales mix.

scenes.heading: Two models, mix 3 Trail : 1 Cargo
scenes.say: Tallgrass sells three Trail bikes for every Cargo bike. A bundle of three Trails and one Cargo contributes three times $900 plus $1,500: $4,200.

scenes.heading: Breakeven
scenes.say: Fixed costs of $540,000 divided by $4,200 gives about a hundred twenty-nine bundles. That's about three hundred eighty-six Trail bikes and a hundred twenty-nine Cargo bikes.
If the mix shifts toward Cargo bikes, which contribute more, breakeven falls. If customers switch to Trail bikes, it rises, even if total units don't change.
And if a resource is scarce, like assembly hours, the best product is the one with the highest contribution per hour of that resource, not per bike. That's Lecture 7.

scenes.q: If the mix were 1 Trail : 1 Cargo, what would the CM per bundle be?
scenes.say: Quick check. If the mix were one Trail to one Cargo, what's the contribution per bundle? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. $900 plus $1,500 is $2,400 per two-bike bundle, so breakeven would be 225 of each.
